solutions.latex:
Read the cumulative frequencies from the graph (the cumulative frequency is the height at the right-hand edge of each column):
$$\begin{array}{c|cccccccc} \text{Downloads} & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 & 7 & 8 & 9 \\ \hline \text{Cumulative frequency} & 17 & 29 & 35 & 47 & 66 & 94 & 99 & 100 \end{array}$$
There are 100 values, so we locate the quartiles at positions 25, 50 and 75.

Lower quartile: the 25th value lies in the group where the cumulative frequency passes 25 (17 at 2, 29 at 3), so $Q_1 = 3$.

Median: the 50th and 51st values lie where it passes 50 (47 at 5, 66 at 6), so the median is $6$.

Upper quartile: the 75th value lies where it passes 75 (66 at 6, 94 at 7), so $Q_3 = 7$.

The minimum is 2 and the maximum is 9.

The five-number summary is $2,\ 3,\ 6,\ 7,\ 9$, which is the box-plot in option C.

parts.latex:
Some data are used to create a box plot shown.

\exfigure{40_q15_1}

A histogram is created from the same set of data.

Which of these histograms is NOT possible for the given box plot?

solutions.latex:
Each histogram has $2+3+2+2+2+3+2 = 16$ scores (the same total in every option), so the quartiles lie between the 4th and 5th, 8th and 9th, and 12th and 13th scores.

On the box plot, the whiskers are short compared with the box: the minimum is about $16\%$ of the range below $Q_1$, and the maximum about $16\%$ above $Q_3$. The median is in the centre of the box.

Test $Q_1$ in each histogram (the 4th and 5th scores).

In A, B and C, the 4th and 5th scores are in the second bar, so $Q_1$ is close to the minimum, as on the box plot.

In D, the bar frequencies are $1, 2, 4, 2, 4, 2, 1$. The cumulative frequencies are $1, 3, 7, \dots$, so the 4th and 5th scores are in the third bar. Then $Q_1$ is more than a quarter of the way along the range, so the lower whisker would be too long. By symmetry the same happens at $Q_3$.

So the box plot cannot come from histogram D.

$$\therefore \text{ Option D is NOT possible.}$$

parts.latex:
Each diagram shows a dot-plot with 15 scores and a box-plot below it.

In which diagram does the box-plot represent the same data as in the dot-plot?

solutions.latex:
A box-plot shows the minimum, $Q_1$, median, $Q_3$ and maximum. For 15 scores, the median is the 8th score, $Q_1$ is the 4th score and $Q_3$ is the 12th score.

Read the dot-plot in diagram A (scores $1$ to $8$, with $2,3,3,4,0,1,0,2$ dots) in order:
$$1,1,2,2,2,3,3,3,4,4,4,4,6,8,8$$
The five-number summary is
$$\text{min}=1,\quad Q_1=2,\quad \text{median}=3,\quad Q_3=4,\quad \text{max}=8$$
These match the box-plot in A: the whisker starts at 1, the box runs from 2 to 4 with the median line at 3, and the upper whisker ends at 8.

The other diagrams do not match:

In B the median score is 6, but the median line is at 5.

In C, $Q_1=4$, but the box starts halfway between 3 and 4.

In D, $Q_1=3$, but the box starts halfway between 2 and 3.

Hence the answer is A.

The sizes, in square metres, of the 21 shops in a small shopping centre are summarised in the following histogram.

\exfigure{830_q28_1}

parts.latex: Using the histogram, determine the average shop area of the shopping centre, correct to 1 decimal place.

The five-number summary of shop areas is given in the following table.

\extable{830_q28_t1}

Determine whether there are any outliers in the data set.

Support your answer with relevant calculations.

Sketch a box-and-whisker plot of the data set.

\exfigure{830_q28_2}
Describe the shape of the distribution of shop areas.

solutions.latex:
Using the histogram, the mean is the sum of the (area $\times$ frequency) values divided by the total frequency.
$$\begin{aligned} \bar{x} &= \dfrac{4\times25+6\times50+75+700+3\times125}{21} \\ &= \dfrac{1550}{21} \\ &\approx 73.8 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$

meta.source_flag: The numerator 4×25+6×50+75+700+3×125 equals 100+300+75+700+375=1550, which is consistent with the source, but the 700 term (a single shop with area 700) cannot be checked against the histogram, which is not shown here.
meta.final_by: claude-sonnet-5-5 26 Nov (read from the worked solution)

solutions.latex:
Outliers lie outside $Q_L-1.5\times IQR$ and $Q_U+1.5\times IQR$.
$$\begin{aligned} IQR &= 101-42 \\ &= 59 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} Q_L-1.5\times IQR &= 42-1.5\times59 \\ &= -46.5 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} Q_U+1.5\times IQR &= 101+1.5\times59 \\ &= 189.5 \end{aligned}$$
There are no scores below $-46.5$ or above $189.5$.

Therefore there are no outliers.

solutions.latex:
From the box and whisker plot, the five-number summary is:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{minimum} &= 30 & Q_1 &= 50 \\ \text{median} &= 65 & Q_3 &\approx 75 \\ \text{maximum} &= 80 \end{aligned}$$
The minimum, $Q_1$, median, $Q_3$ and maximum divide the data into four parts, each containing 25% of the residents.

The lower whisker runs from $30$ to $50$, so this age group contains 25% of the residents.

The other options are not one of the four quarters: $50 - 75$ contains 50%, and $65 - 80$ contains about 50%. $70 - 80$ does not start at a marked value.

Hence the correct option is A.

figures.cap: parallel box plots for Vitamin A and Vitamin B

parts.latex:
A new drug study was conducted with 80 people chosen at random to determine whether taking Vitamin $A$ or Vitamin $B$ over a period of 2 months, had any significant effects on lowering cholesterol levels.

40 people were given Vitamin $A$ and the other 40 people were given Vitamin $B$.

All 80 people recorded cholesterol levels between 8 and 10 before the study.

The diagram below shows parallel box plots with the results of the study from the two groups.

\exfigure{235_q27_1}

By comparing the differences in the presented data (in terms of central tendency and spread), what conclusions can be made about the effectiveness of the Vitamins in the study?

solutions.latex:
Reading the box plots (approximately):

Vitamin $A$: minimum $5.2$, $Q_1 = 6.5$, median $7.6$, $Q_3 = 7.9$, maximum $10$.

Vitamin $B$: minimum $3.2$, $Q_1 = 4.5$, median $5$, $Q_3 = 6$, maximum $8$.

Central tendency: everyone started between $8$ and $10$. Vitamin $B$ has median $5$ compared with $7.6$ for Vitamin $A$, and its whole box and most of its data lie lower. Both groups' medians are below $8$, but Vitamin $B$ lowered cholesterol by much more.

Spread: the ranges are about the same ($4.8$ for both) and the interquartile ranges are similar ($1.4$ for $A$, $1.5$ for $B$), so the variability of results is similar.

Conclusion: both vitamins appear to lower cholesterol, but Vitamin $B$ is more effective as its median and quartiles are much lower, while the spread is similar. (Vitamin $A$ had a maximum of $10$, so for some people it may have had no effect.)
criteria: Compares both the central tendency and the spread, or equivalent merit
Compares the medians or the spread correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Reading the five-number summaries from the box-plot:

Home: minimum $25$, $Q_1=35$, median $65$, $Q_3=80$, maximum $95$.

Away: minimum $20$, $Q_1=25$, median $35$, $Q_3=60$, maximum $80$.

Skewness: the home median ($65$) is closer to $Q_3$ than $Q_1$, with a longer lower tail, so the home distribution is negatively skewed. The away median ($35$) is closer to $Q_1$, with a longer upper part, so the away distribution is positively skewed.

Central tendency: the home median ($65$) is much higher than the away median ($35$), so the team generally scores higher at home.

Spread: the home interquartile range is $80-35=45$ and the range is $95-25=70$. The away interquartile range is $60-25=35$ and the range is $80-20=60$. The home scores are more spread out.
criteria: Compares two of skewness, central tendency and spread, with supporting values, or equivalent merit
